title: Area and Volume
subtitle: Master area, surface area, volume formulas, and scaling relationships

sections.title: Key Formulas
sections.content:
The SAT provides a reference sheet with most geometry formulas. But knowing them cold saves time.

**Area:**
- Rectangle: $A = lw$
- Square: $A = s^2$
- Triangle: $A = \frac{1}{2}bh$
- Circle: $A = \pi r^2$

**Volume:**
- Rectangular prism: $V = lwh$
- Cube: $V = s^3$
- Cylinder: $V = \pi r^2 h$
- Cone: $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$
- Sphere: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$

**Circumference:** $C = 2\pi r$

sections.title: Surface Area = Sum of All Face Areas
sections.content:
For a rectangular box (prism):
$$SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)$$

For a cube with side $s$:
$$SA = 6s^2 \quad \text{(6 square faces)}$$

For a box WITHOUT a lid: subtract one face from the full surface area.

sections.title: Example: Surface Area Without a Lid
sections.problem: A box with no lid has edge length 29 inches (all faces are squares). What is the exterior surface area?

steps.description: A cube has 6 faces. A box without a lid has 5 faces

sections.title: Type 4: Setting Two Area Expressions Equal
Example: Find the Square with the Same Area as a Circle
sections.problem: What is the side length of a square with the same area as a circle with radius 2?

steps.description: Set equal to square area: s² = 4π

sections.title: Type 5: Scaling — How Area and Volume Change with Size
The Scaling Rules
sections.content:
When you scale all dimensions of a shape by a factor $k$:
- **Length** scales by $k$
- **Area** scales by $k^2$ (because area involves two dimensions)
- **Volume** scales by $k^3$ (because volume involves three dimensions)

This is one of the most important rules for the SAT geometry section.

sections.title: Example: Scaling Area
sections.problem: Square A has side lengths 166 times those of Square B. The area of Square A is $k$ times the area of Square B. What is $k$?

steps.description: Side length ratio = 166. Area scales by the square of the side ratio

sections.tip: Area scales as the square of any linear dimension. If sides are 3× longer, area is 9× larger.

sections.title: Example: Scale from Perimeter
sections.problem: Square X has side length 12 cm. Square Y has perimeter 2 times the perimeter of Square X. What is the side length of Square Y?

steps.description: Perimeter of X = 4 × 12 = 48 cm. Perimeter of Y = 2 × 48 = 96 cm

sections.answer: Side length of Square Y = $24$ cm

sections.title: Example: Area of a Composite Figure
sections.problem: [IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: Composite shape made of a rectangle and a semicircle on top]. The rectangle is 10 × 6 and the semicircle has diameter 6. Find the total area.
sections.tip: For compound shapes: divide into familiar pieces, find each area, and add (or subtract if one shape is cut out of another).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: **Scaling:** area scales as $k^2$; volume scales as $k^3$ when linear dimensions scale by $k$
**Surface area without lid:** subtract one face from total

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Confusing radius and diameter in circle formulas (radius = diameter ÷ 2)
- Forgetting $\pi$ in area or circumference of circles
- Using area formula for volume or vice versa (especially for cylinders)
- Scaling area by $k$ instead of $k^2$
- Forgetting to subtract the lid face when computing open-box surface area

sat_tips: The SAT formula sheet is available during the test — use it for volume formulas you don't know cold
For scaling: if the problem says side lengths increase by a factor k, area increases by k² and volume by k³
For surface area of a lidless box: 5s² instead of 6s²
Equating two area formulas is common — set them equal and solve for the unknown
